summary:
Recommendation: move the wordpress MySQL database to three AWS services in three waves. Wave 1 moves it to Aurora MySQL, which ends up serving 63.6% of the queries; wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 22 hot reads (79.4% of calls); wave 3 moves 36.4% of the queries to DynamoDB. The projected cost of the full modernization is $758 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-11-04. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is high. The main exposure is a high-severity migration complexity risk on Aurora MySQL: review it in the risk register before wave 1 starts.

Decision: no wave is suggested yet. Waves 1, 2 and 3 are not designed yet: run their schema design.
summary_deterministic: Analyzed 50 source tables and 107 query patterns across 3 target database(s). Workload split: Aurora MySQL handles 68 queries (63.6%), DynamoDB handles 39 queries (36.4%). Cache layer: ElastiCache fronts 22 designed cached reads (79.4% of calls) cache-aside, as recommended for hot, small reads; their owner engines stay the system of record. Estimated monthly cost: $757.62. 6 open migration risks (overall: HIGH); 4 more were resolved by the assignment. Top query groups by throughput: wordpress.wp_postmeta, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta, wordpress.wp_term_taxonomy (+2 more). Other targets evaluated: DocumentDB (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check), OpenSearch (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check).

These reads total 194.334 calls/s, above the 1 calls/s hot-read floor.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Not checked: schema design was not run for DynamoDB, so 20 queries assigned to it have no access pattern to check against: UPDATE `wp_woocommerce_api_keys` SET `last_access` = ? WHERE `key_id` = ?; SELECT `key_id` , `user_id` , `permissions` , `consumer_key` , `consumer_secr...; DELETE FROM `wp_options` WHERE `option_name` = ?; and 17 more
risks.mitigation: Run the DynamoDB schema design; any of these queries it does not serve then becomes a schema design gap. Start with the tables the most of them touch: wordpress.wp_options (6), wordpress.wp_comments (3), wordpress.wp_termmeta (3).

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 55 queries read 15 tables on an engine that does not own them. 52 of them read a copy of 13 tables that CDC keeps current from DynamoDB across 1 engine pair, so a read there can miss a recent write. The other 2 tables are written by no captured query, so a one-time copy serves them.
risks.mitigation: Before Wave 3 starts, set up CDC for each engine pair the sources of truth section lists, and send any read that must see its own write to its source of truth; copy the read-only tables once and confirm nothing outside the captured workload writes them. Compare the row counts on both sides. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 19 queries were decided by less than 5 points, and 5 more were exact ties a routing rule settled: Aurora MySQL keeps 15 close calls and 5 ties over DynamoDB; DynamoDB takes 4 close calls over Aurora MySQL. A small change in the scores moves them.
risks.mitigation: Confirm the engine for these queries in the assignment review before Wave 3 starts, using the close calls section; move any that fit the runner-up better.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Routing did not penalise DynamoDB for the frequent-full-scan finding the source shows on 1 query, because the design removes the read it is about (each query's evidence says how).
details: A whole read of a small reference table, which the design keeps as one item collection or caches.
risks.mitigation: Design this query in DynamoDB as each one's evidence says, and serve none of them as a scan. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: [aurora_mysql] We could not translate 1 routine automatically; migrate it yourself before wave 1. It is 1 procedure. This is a to-do and holds no wave. Why: a check failed (1).
details: mysql-routine-set-global: Setting a global or persisted system variable needs SUPER or SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN, which the Aurora MySQL administrative role (rds_superuser_role) does not include, so the statement fails when the routine runs. Fix: Set the variable in the DB cluster or DB parameter group instead, or set its session value if the routine only needs it for itself.
risks.mitigation: Migrate this routine yourself before wave 1, then check it again. See the Wave 1 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: [aurora_mysql] Wave 1: 1 routine is carried to Aurora MySQL and need a check on the target: 1 has a safe header rewrite (the owner or DEFINER set to the target user, so it runs with that user's privileges).
risks.mitigation: Check the carried routines when they are deployed on Aurora MySQL in step 1, and that the target user's privileges cover what each rewritten one does. See the Wave 1 gate in the roadmap.

mitigation_strategies: After wave 1 (Aurora MySQL): compare the latency of 107 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 1.16 ms) and check the engine sustains the collected traffic of 142 requests/s before starting wave 2.
After wave 2 (ElastiCache): track the cache hit rate for the 22 hot reads it fronts on Aurora MySQL (79.4% of calls, 194.3 calls/s) and compare their latency with the source before starting wave 3.
After wave 3 (DynamoDB): compare the latency of 39 queries with their source baseline.

Aurora serves these reads natively and its query optimizer adds nothing to them (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora).

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] GROUP BY, HAVING, or an aggregate over rows no key anchors or over a join (one key's COUNT or SUM is a Query on that key, not this pattern). DynamoDB has no server-side aggregation: a Query or Scan can only count the items it reads (Select = COUNT), so a grouped result needs the application layer, pre-computed aggregates or a separate analytics store (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, Query).

migration_waves.title: Move to Aurora MySQL
migration_waves.rationale: The whole source database (MySQL 8.0.45) moves 1:1 to Aurora MySQL: same engine family. The collector reports engine and version only; feature compatibility is not assessed here. 68 queries (63.6%) remain on Aurora MySQL once later waves have moved their share; later waves move subsets of these 50 tables and views out of Aurora MySQL.
migration_waves.gate: Schema and data parity validated against the source database. Decommission the source MySQL database once you have completed your cutover: later waves move from Aurora MySQL, not from it. The cutover is your responsibility. Close RISK-006 before this gate (carried routines to check). To do before wave 1: migrate 1 routine yourself (RISK-005).

migration_waves.title: Cache hot reads with ElastiCache
migration_waves.rationale: 22 hot reads (79.4% of calls), cache-aside in front of Aurora MySQL in wave 2, then DynamoDB once wave 3 moves these reads: no data migration, fully reversible. It takes the read pressure off before the data migrations that follow. These reads belong to queries that move in wave 1 (Aurora MySQL) and wave 3 (DynamoDB); this share overlaps the owner shares, which alone sum to 100%.

migration_waves.title: Move key-value and point-lookup queries to DynamoDB
migration_waves.rationale: 39 key-value and point-lookup queries (36.4% of queries) across 1 table group, where co-dependent tables move together: the pattern DynamoDB fits best, and the smallest-blast-radius data migration available once the cache wave has absorbed the read pressure.
migration_waves.gate: Dual-write/backfill validated and query parity confirmed per table group. 13 of the 15 tables moving to DynamoDB (wordpress.wp_actionscheduler_actions, wordpress.wp_actionscheduler_logs, wordpress.wp_comments, wordpress.wp_options, wordpress.wp_postmeta, wordpress.wp_posts, wordpress.wp_termmeta, wordpress.wp_wc_product_meta_lookup, wordpress.wp_wc_reserved_stock, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_api_keys, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_downloadable_product_permissions, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_order_items) stay dual-read by Aurora MySQL queries, which remain on Aurora MySQL; DynamoDB owns them, so keep the Aurora MySQL copy current from DynamoDB via CDC. The other 2 tables (wordpress.wp_commentmeta, wordpress.wp_wc_tax_rate_classes) move with no further Aurora MySQL reads. 3 queries read 2 tables (wordpress.wp_term_relationships, wordpress.wp_users) Aurora MySQL owns (wave 1) and keeps owning; keep a DynamoDB copy of them current via CDC. cache_layer.role_sentence: ElastiCache is recommended as a cache-aside layer in front of the engine that owns each cached read: the cached reads are hot, small and can be rebuilt from that engine, so it stays the system of record and the cache is sized for the hot reads, not the whole dataset. ElastiCache for Valkey 9.0 and later offers durability on Multi-AZ clusters; this assessment does not use it as a system of record today.

why: A check failed: Setting a global or persisted system variable needs SUPER or SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN, which the Aurora MySQL administrative role (rds_superuser_role) does not include, so the statement fails when the routine runs. Fix: Set the variable in the DB cluster or DB parameter group instead, or set its session value if the routine only needs it for itself.

check_notes.label: DEFINER set to the target user
check_notes.text: A DEFINER naming an account that does not exist on the target makes every call fail with error 1449, so the DEFINER clause is rewritten to the user that creates the routine on Aurora MySQL; only that clause of the header changes, never the body; a routine that runs as its definer (SQL SECURITY DEFINER, and every trigger and event) then runs with the target user's privileges, and its record says so.

architectural_patterns.name: Event-Driven Sync
architectural_patterns.description: Use database change streams or event logs to propagate changes between databases asynchronously. Each database maintains its own optimized representation of the data.
architectural_patterns.when: Multiple engines need the same data in different shapes
architectural_patterns.example: Change data capture on DynamoDB carries each committed change to Aurora MySQL. Each consumer shapes the data for its own access patterns.

recommendations: Consolidated 8 queries from DocumentDB → Aurora MySQL: DocumentDB provides no unique capabilities over Aurora MySQL. No saving is claimed: DocumentDB does not run today; it was a candidate this plan considered and does not recommend.
Consolidated 3 queries from DocumentDB → DynamoDB: DocumentDB provides no unique capabilities over DynamoDB. DocumentDB does not run today, so no saving is claimed.

Consolidated 1 query from OpenSearch → Aurora MySQL: OpenSearch provides no unique capabilities over Aurora MySQL. No saving is claimed: OpenSearch was never justified by the workload. None of its first-assignment queries clear the real-search-depth plus traffic-or-result-size floor a standing deployment needs, so no infrastructure cost was ever justified for it.

Recommended pattern: Event-Driven Sync. Use database change streams or event logs to propagate changes between databases asynchronously. Each database maintains its own optimized representation of the data.
